endorsements.title: Developing, purchasing, implementing and monitoring AI tools in radiology: practical considerations. A multi-society statement
endorsements.issuer: ACR, CAR, ESR, RANZCR, RSNA; Radiol Artif Intell 2024 (PMID 38251899, doi:10.1148/ryai.230513)
endorsements.quote: There has been much comment about the black box nature of AI models, with early efforts focused on heat map and saliency visualizations; some researchers have called for a combination of visualizations and generated text to improve interpretability of diagnoses (35–37).

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Share transparency reports with internal and external stakeholders that detail steps taken to update the GAI system to enhance transparency and accountability.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Consider whether transparency measures have been defined to provide different user-facing views of model outcomes (e.g., options vs. automatically ranked or triaged), thereby ensuring that interpretation bias is mitigated.

endorsements.title: Implementing Artificial Intelligence in Critical Care Medicine: a consensus of 22
endorsements.quote: A straightforward example of the latter is the development of interpretable, real-time dashboards that synthetize complex multidimensional data into visual formats, thereby enhancing clinicians’ situational awareness without overwhelming them.

evidence.title: ContextualSHAP : Enhancing SHAP Explanations Through Contextual Language Generation
evidence.outcome: Perceived understandability of SHAP explanations with LLM text plus visuals versus visual-only
evidence.effect: Generated contextual text explanations were perceived as more understandable and contextually appropriate than visual-only outputs (Likert surveys and interviews; preliminary findings).
evidence.quote: The results, based on Likert-scale surveys and follow-up interviews, indicate that the generated explanations were perceived as more understandable and contextually appropriate compared to visual-only outputs.

evidence.title: Non-task expert physicians benefit from correct explainable AI advice when reviewing X-rays
evidence.outcome: Physician diagnostic accuracy with vs without visual annotation on X-ray advice
evidence.effect: Annotated advice raised accuracy overall (OR 2.30, p=0.002); IM/EM physicians improved by 5.66% (p=0.042); radiologists 3.41% (p=0.120, non-significant).
evidence.quote: When looking at the results separated by task expertise (defined by discipline), we found that providing annotated advice improved the mean performance of the IM/EM physicians in our experiment by 5.66% ( p = 0.042, see Fig. 2 a).

evidence.title: Can incorrect artificial intelligence (AI) results impact radiologists, and if so, what can we do about it? A multi-reader pilot study of lung cancer detection with chest radiography
evidence.outcome: False negatives with visual AI output
evidence.effect: FNs were 33.0% without box vs. 20.7% with box, p = 0.04.
evidence.quote: As anticipated in hypothesis 5, FNs were higher in AI Keep (No Box) than in AI Keep (Box) (33.0% vs. 20.7%, p = 0.04).
evidence.sample_unit: radiologists (each reading 90 chest radiographs across 4 conditions)

evidence.title: Impact of Different Artificial Intelligence User Interfaces on Lung Nodule and Mass Detection on Chest Radiographs
evidence.effect: Text-only improved performance; confidence/text and overlay UIs did not, while 8/10 radiologists (80%) preferred the overlay UI.
evidence.quote: Text-only UI output significantly improved radiologist performance compared with no AI in the detection of lung nodules and masses on chest radiographs, but user preference did not correspond with user performance.

evidence.title: Visualizing machine learning-based predictions of postpartum depression risk for lay audiences
evidence.outcome: Risk classification accuracy and perceptions across four presentation formats of ML risk output
evidence.effect: Classification performance was high (93%) with no significant differences between presentation formats; inconsistent differences in perceived risk, trust, and behavioral intention; gradient number line most preferred (43%).
evidence.quote: For the risk classification question, performance was high (93%) with no significant differences between presentation formats.

evidence.title: Evaluating cognitive biases in AI-assisted mammography interpretation: a simulation reader study of explainable AI across radiologist experience levels
evidence.effect: With XAI, automation and anchoring bias decreased to 32/180 (17.8%) and 31/180 (17.2%), respectively.
evidence.quote: With XAI, these rates decreased to 32/180 (17.8%) and 31/180 (17.2%), respectively.
evidence.sample_unit: radiologists (200 mammograms each, three sequential reading conditions)

evidence.title: Divergent impacts of explainable AI for dermatological diagnosis on clinicians versus lay people
evidence.outcome: Effect of different explanation formats (basic, GradCAM, CBIR, LLM) on user accuracy and deference
evidence.effect: LLM explanations gave largest lay gain (+7.7%) but largest loss when wrong; for PCPs LLM was least helpful (+17.7%) though improving confidence calibration (r=0.494).
evidence.quote: Interestingly, for PCPs, LLM explanations were the least helpful method (+17.7%) and were 8.1% lower than the best improvement from the basic explanations ( β = −0.081, 95% CI: −0.207 to 0.044, P = 0.268; Fig. 3b and Supplementary Table 16 ).

evidence.title: Development and validation of Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) and GraphRAG for complex clinical cases
evidence.effect: GraphRAG scored lower in clarity because long guideline excerpts obscured key recommendations.
evidence.quote: However, GraphRAG scored lower in clarity, as its graph walks often returned long guideline excerpts that obscured key recommendations.

evidence.title: Explainable AI as a Double-Edged Sword in Dermatology: The Impact on Clinicians versus The Public
evidence.outcome: diagnostic accuracy by suggestion presentation order when AI was incorrect
evidence.effect: Presenting AI suggestions first led to worse outcomes when AI was incorrect for both groups
evidence.quote: Presenting AI suggestions first also led to worse outcomes when the AI was incorrect for both groups.

evidence.title: The explainable AI dilemma under knowledge imbalance in specialist AI for glaucoma referrals in primary care
evidence.effect: Both intrinsic and post-hoc explanation types contributed to anchoring bias toward AI referrals.
evidence.quote: Post-hoc explanations increased over-reliance on incorrect AI recommendations, and both explanation types contributed to anchoring bias, making participants align more closely with AI referrals than without explanations.

evidence.title: Evaluating the interpretability of clinical speech AI models: Lessons from two user studies
evidence.effect: Bar-chart presentation frequently caused feature influence to be interpreted as clinical severity; no numeric rate reported.
evidence.quote: The seemingly intuitive bar-chart design frequently misled participating speech-language pathology (SLP) students to interpret feature influence as an indicator of clinical severity.

commentary.bottom_line: Five simulated studies suggest that adding visual annotations or explanatory text to AI output may improve reader accuracy and reduce anchoring, but one large study found that LLM explanations also produced the largest losses when the AI was wrong. No study tested unranked option formats, and no study measured patient outcomes in live care.

perspectives.view: All five tests are level 4 offline or simulated studies. Two enrolled 6 or fewer readers, and one did not report its sample. Results agree for visual annotation (OR 2.30; false negatives 33.0% versus 20.7%) but are mixed for text explanations. Indirect outcomes, small samples, and inconsistency support very low certainty.

Bounding boxes lowered radiologist false negatives from 33.0% to 20.7%. In one reader study, explainable output reduced automation bias to 17.8% of decisions and anchoring bias to 17.2%. LLM explanations produced the largest lay loss when the AI was wrong, which suggests persuasive text may increase deference to incorrect output.

The benefit appears to depend on the user. Annotated advice improved accuracy for internal and emergency medicine physicians by 5.66%, while radiologists gained a non-significant 3.41%. Among the formats tested, LLM text helped primary care physicians least. A preliminary survey found text plus visuals more understandable, but perceived understanding may not predict accuracy.

No test reported enrolling Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy users. The one study with lay participants found that LLM explanations gave both the largest gain (+7.7%) and the largest loss when the AI was wrong. In one hazard study, readers took bar-chart feature influence to mean clinical severity.

The endorsements come from voluntary frameworks and professional statements. CHAI asks developers to consider option views versus ranked or triaged views to reduce interpretation bias, and NIST calls for transparency reports. None of the supplied sources sets a binding display standard.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared unranked option lists with ranked or triaged output, and every test used offline cases with clinician or lay raters. Prospective studies in live workflows should measure diagnostic error and patient outcomes. They should also test whether text explanations raise deference when the AI is wrong. Display order needs study as well, since one hazard study linked AI-first presentation to worse accuracy when the AI was incorrect.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the five tests reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and two did not report their setting. Health systems serving these groups have no evidence that the reported accuracy gains apply to their users, particularly for text explanations shown to patients.
